subtopic: Nature of Roots and Boundary Conditions
working: Equal roots require the discriminant to vanish: (8k)^2 - 4*k*32 = 64k^2 - 128k = 64k(k-2) = 0, so k = 0 or k = 2. k = 0 kills the x^2 term and leaves 32 = 0, which is not a quadratic with equal roots, so k = 2.
Put t = x^2: t^2 - 5t + 6 = 0 gives t = 2, 3, so x^2 = 2 or x^2 = 3 and x = +/-sqrt(2), +/-sqrt(3). Option (A) is the distractor that forgets to take the square root.

Real coefficients force the conjugate 3+4i to be the other root, so sum = 6 = -b/a giving b = -6a, and product = 9+16 = 25 = c/a giving c = 25a. Then 31a + b + c = 31a - 6a + 25a = 50a, and 2c = 2(25a) = 50a, so the value equals 2c (2b = -12a and 2a are both wrong).

subtopic: Nature of Roots and Boundary Conditions
working: Equal roots in x^2+bx+a=0 give b^2 = 4a and the repeated root r = -b/2; substituting r into ax^2+x+b=0 gives ab^2/4 + b/2 = 0, i.e. b = 0 or ab = -2. b=0 forces a=0 (both equations then have root 0), and ab=-2 with a=b^2/4 gives b^3=-8, so b=-2, a=1 (checked: x^2-2x+1 has the double root 1, and x^2+x-2 has roots 1 and -2, common root 1). Both branches give 2a^2 + b = 0.

subtopic: Nature of Roots and Boundary Conditions
working: x^2+1 > 0 for every real x, so the inequality may be cross-multiplied without a sign split: 2(x+2) > x^2+1 gives x^2 - 2x - 3 < 0, i.e. (x-3)(x+1) < 0 and -1 < x < 3. The integers strictly inside are 0, 1, 2 — three of them.

2x = -1 + i*sqrt(3) makes x = w, a primitive cube root of unity, so 1 + w + w^2 = 0. Then 1 + x - x^2 = 1 + w - w^2 = -2w^2 and 1 - x + x^2 = 1 - w + w^2 = -2w. Sixth powers: (-2w^2)^6 = 64*w^12 = 64 and (-2w)^6 = 64*w^6 = 64, so the difference is 64 - 64 = 0 (verified symbolically).
notes: 2x = -1 + i*sqrt3 makes x a primitive cube root of unity, so 1 + x - x^2 = -2w^2 and 1 - x + x^2 = -2w. Both sixth powers are 64, and the stem subtracts them, so the value is 0. Verified numerically: the expression evaluates to 7e-15

working: z+1 = (z+4) - 3, so |z+1| <= |z+4| + 3 <= 3 + 3 = 6, and the bound is attained: z = -7 satisfies |z+4| = 3 and gives |z+1| = 6. That single witness also falsifies (A) <=5 and (B) <=4, so only <=6 holds for all admissible z.

With z = x+iy, z^2 + |z|^2 = (x^2-y^2+2ixy) + (x^2+y^2) = 2x^2 + 2ixy. Both parts vanish iff x = 0 (which makes the imaginary part 0 automatically), leaving y free: every purely imaginary z = iy is a solution, so there are infinitely many.

Writing z = x+iy the equation becomes x^2 + y^2 + 4x + 6y + 4 = 0 (the imaginary parts cancel identically), i.e. (x+2)^2 + (y+3)^2 = 9. Radius = 3. Equivalently, for z*zbar + abar*z + a*zbar + b = 0 with a = 2+3i, b = 4, radius = sqrt(|a|^2 - b) = sqrt(13-4) = 3.

If the two classes meet at the same hour no student can attend both, so the sets are disjoint and |C union P| = 20 + 30 = 50, making (A) true. If they meet at different hours the ten double-enrolled students are counted twice, so |C union P| = 20 + 30 - 10 = 40, making (B) true. Both statements hold, so (C).
65% own neither, so |C union S| = 35%. Inclusion-exclusion gives |C and S| = 25 + 15 - 35 = 5%. If 5% of the total is 1500 families then the total is 1500/0.05 = 30000.

subtopic: Relations — Properties, Cartesian Product, and Counting
working: A = {x in Z : |x| < 3} = {-2,-1,0,1,2}. Pairing each x with y = |x| (and |x| lies in A for every such x) gives R = {(-2,2),(-1,1),(0,0),(1,1),(2,2)}, which is the set listed in (A). (C) wrongly drops the negative preimages.
notes: Option (A) is printed with a missing opening parenthesis on its first pair ('{ - 2,2),...'); the intended set is unambiguous and no other option matches it, so this is a typesetting artefact rather than a defect that changes the answer.

working: Replacing x by -x gives 2f(-x) + 3f(x) = 15 + 4x. Solving the pair {2u+3v = 15-4x, 3u+2v = 15+4x} for u = f(x) gives 5u = 15 + 20x, so f(x) = 4x + 3 (checked back in the original relation), and f(2) = 11.

Cutting squares of side x gives V = x(24-2x)^2 on 0 < x < 12. V' = (24-2x)(24-6x), whose interior zero is x = 4 (x = 12 is the degenerate endpoint with V = 0). V(4) = 4*16^2 = 1024 is the maximum, so the height is 4 cm.

subtopic: Nature of Roots and Boundary Conditions
working: Left inequality: x^2+4x+4 > 9x-2 gives x^2-5x+6 > 0, so x < 2 or x > 3. Right inequality: x^2+4x+4 < 12x-3 gives x^2-8x+7 < 0, so 1 < x < 7. The intersection is (1,2) union (3,7); (1,2) contains no integer and (3,7) contains 4, 5, 6 — three integral values.

x - [x] is the fractional part, so f(x) = {x} + 3 and f(x+1) = {x+1} + 3 = {x} + 3 = f(x); no smaller positive period exists because {x} rises from 0 to 1 once per unit interval. It is a genuine function (so not (A)), its period is 1 not pi (so not (B)), and it is many-to-one hence non-invertible (so not (D)).

log_4[(x^3+x^2)/(x+1)] = log_4[x^2(x+1)/(x+1)] = log_4(x^2) = 2, so x^2 = 16 and x = 4 given x > 0 (x = -4 is rejected by the stated domain, and it also makes the original logarithm arguments negative).

f(x+y) + f(x-y) = [a^(x+y) + a^(-x-y) + a^(x-y) + a^(-x+y)]/2, while 2f(x)f(y) = 2*(a^x+a^-x)(a^y+a^-y)/4 = [a^(x+y) + a^(x-y) + a^(-x+y) + a^(-x-y)]/2 — the same four terms. Checked numerically at an awkward point (a = 3.5, x = 3/7, y = -5/11): both sides give 2.677544..., while f(x)f(y) = 1.3388 and f(x)-f(y) = -0.0189 do not match.

LHS = ((a^2-b^2)^2)^(x-1) = (a-b)^(2x-2)*(a+b)^(2x-2). Equating with (a-b)^(2x)*(a+b)^(-2) and cancelling gives (a+b)^(2x) = (a-b)^2, so 2x*log(a+b) = 2*log|a-b| and x = log|a-b|/log(a+b). Verified numerically: for (a,b) = (5,2) and (9,4), only candidate D makes both sides agree to 10 significant figures; A, B and C all fail.
notes: the left side is ((a^2-b^2)^2)^(x-1). Taking logs, (x-1)(log|a-b| + log(a+b)) = 2x*log|a-b|/2 - log(a+b) reduces to x*log(a+b) = log|a-b|, so x = log|a-b| / log(a+b). Matching exponents termwise is NOT available here — it gives -2 = 0 — which is why the log route is the intended one

working: 3x^2 - 4x + 5 has discriminant 16 - 60 = -44 < 0 with a positive leading coefficient, so it is strictly positive for every real x (its minimum value is 11/3 at x = 2/3). The square root is therefore defined on all of R.

3x^2-4x+5 has discriminant 16-60 = -44 < 0 so it is always positive; its minimum is at x = 2/3 with value 5 - 4/3 = 11/3, so the quadratic ranges over [11/3, inf). g[f(x)] = log_e (f(x))^2 = log_e (3x^2-4x+5), whose range is therefore [log_e(11/3), inf).
notes: g[f(x)] = log_e(f(x)^2) = log_e(3x^2 - 4x + 5). That quadratic has its minimum at x = 2/3 with value 11/3 and is unbounded above, so the range is [log_e(11/3), infinity)

working: ARRANGE has 7 letters with A twice and R twice, so total arrangements = 7!/(2!2!) = 1260. Treating RR as one block gives 6!/2! = 360 arrangements with the R's together, so never together = 1260 - 360 = 900. Confirmed by brute-force enumeration of all distinct permutations.
A's together (AA as one block, R still doubled) = 6!/2! = 360; both A's and R's together = 5! = 120. So A's together but R's apart = 360 - 120 = 240. Brute-force enumeration gives 240.
Inclusion-exclusion on the total 1260: |A together| = 360, |R together| = 360, |both together| = 120, so neither = 1260 - 360 - 360 + 120 = 660. Brute-force enumeration gives 660.

The sum expands to 50C4 + 55C3 + 54C3 + 53C3 + 52C3 + 51C3 + 50C3. Applying Pascal's rule repeatedly from the bottom: 50C4+50C3 = 51C4, +51C3 = 52C4, ... , +55C3 = 56C4. Evaluated numerically the expression equals 367290 = 56C4.
Boy-vs-boy matches = 7 x 4 = 28; girl-vs-girl matches = n x 6. Total 28 + 6n = 52 gives 6n = 24, so n = 4.

For k >= 5, k! contains both 3 and 5 as factors so k! is divisible by 15. Hence the sum reduces mod 15 to 1! + 2! + 3! + 4! = 1 + 2 + 6 + 24 = 33, and 33 mod 15 = 3. Confirmed by direct computation of the full sum modulo 15.
notes: 15 divides n! for every n >= 5, so only 1!+2!+3!+4! = 33 survives, and 33 mod 15 = 3. Confirmed by computing the full 95-term sum

working: cos(x^2) is not periodic: if f(x+T) = f(x) for all x then x^2 and (x+T)^2 would have to differ by a fixed multiple of 2*pi for every x, but (x+T)^2 - x^2 = 2Tx + T^2 grows without bound with x. The gaps between successive zeros of cos(x^2) shrink as x increases, so no period exists.
The k-th term is 1/(1+2+...+k) = 2/(k(k+1)) = 2(1/k - 1/(k+1)). Telescoping k = 1 to 100 gives 2(1 - 1/101) = 200/101. Exact rational summation confirms 200/101.

subtopic: Coefficients and Specific Terms in Expansion
working: With m = 2n the AP condition 2*C(m,2) = C(m,1) + C(m,3) reduces to (m-2)(m-7) = 0, i.e. m^2 - 9m + 14 = 0. Substituting m = 2n gives 4n^2 - 18n + 14 = 0, so 2n^2 - 9n = -7. Both admissible roots (m = 2 and m = 7) give the same value -7, so the answer is unambiguous.
notes: C(2n,1), C(2n,2), C(2n,3) in AP gives (2n)^2 - 9(2n) + 14 = 0, i.e. 2n^2 - 9n + 7 = 0, so the requested 2n^2 - 9n = -7. Confirmed by scanning m = 2n for 2*C(m,2) = C(m,1) + C(m,3): the only admissible root is m = 7

subtopic: Coefficients and Specific Terms in Expansion
working: Setting x = y = z = 1 gives the sum of coefficients (1-2+3)^n = 2^n = 128, so n = 7. In (1+x)^7 the greatest coefficient is C(7,3) = C(7,4) = 35.
notes: setting x = y = z = 1 gives the coefficient sum (1-2+3)^n = 2^n = 128, so n = 7; the greatest binomial coefficient of (1+x)^7 is C(7,3) = 35

working: AB exists requires cols(A) = rows(B): x + 5 = y. BA exists requires cols(B) = rows(A): 11 - y = x. Substituting, 11 - (x+5) = x gives 6 = 2x, so x = 3 (and y = 8).
Same two conditions as Q33: x + 5 = y and 11 - y = x. Solving gives x = 3, y = 8.

Column 2 is exactly 2 x column 1: (10,-4,-2) = 2(5,-2,-1). Two proportional columns force the determinant to be 0 regardless of b, so the matrix is singular for any value of b. Symbolic expansion of the determinant returns 0 identically.

det A = 6. For 3x3, adj(adj A) = |A|^(n-2) A = 6A, so (adj(adj A))^-1 = (1/6)A^-1 = (1/6)(adj A / 6) = (1/36) adj A. Computing adj A gives [[13,-9,1],[4,0,-2],[-5,3,1]], matching option C. Verified by explicitly inverting adj(adj A) symbolically.

subtopic: Linear Systems — Consistency, Cramer's Rule, Solution Space
working: The coefficient determinant is 0 (rank 2), but the augmented matrix has rank 3. Concretely, R2 - 3R1 gives -11(y-z) = -2 i.e. y-z = 2/11, while R3 - 2R1 gives -5(y-z) = -1 i.e. y-z = 1/5; these contradict, so the system is inconsistent and has no solution.

subtopic: Special Determinants — Trig, Complex, Roots of Unity, Polynomial
working: Expanding along the third column, the cofactors give -cos((alpha+beta)-alpha) + sin((alpha+beta)-alpha) + (cos^2 alpha + sin^2 alpha), so the determinant equals 1 + sin beta - cos beta. Every alpha cancels, so the value depends only on beta, i.e. it is independent of alpha. Symbolic simplification returns 1 - sqrt(2) cos(beta + pi/4), which is the same expression and contains no alpha.

subtopic: Special Determinants — Trig, Complex, Roots of Unity, Polynomial
working: Expanding along row 1 with w^3 = 1: the (1,1) term gives a(c^2 - ab w^3) = a(c^2 - ab); the (1,2) minor is bcw - bc w^4 = 0 since w^4 = w, so that term vanishes; the (1,3) term gives aw * w^2(ab - c^2) = a(ab - c^2). The first and third cancel exactly, so the determinant is 0. Confirmed by symbolic evaluation with w = -1/2 + i sqrt(3)/2.
notes: Stem says 'imaginary root of unity'; read as an imaginary CUBE root of unity (w^3 = 1, w != 1), which the entries' w^2 pattern requires.

working: Columns 2 and 3 of the printed matrix are identical (both read a+2, a+3, a+4 down the rows), and a determinant with two equal columns is 0. Expanded symbolically in sympy for general a it returns exactly 0.
notes: columns 2 and 3 of the determinant are identical ((a+2), (a+3), (a+4) in both), so it vanishes for every a. Verified numerically at a = 3.7

working: With A+B+C = pi, cos C = -cos(A+B) = sinA sinB - cosA cosB, i.e. z + xy = sqrt((1-x^2)(1-y^2)). Squaring gives z^2 + 2xyz + x^2y^2 = 1 - x^2 - y^2 + x^2y^2, so x^2+y^2+z^2 = 1 - 2xyz. Checked numerically at three awkward (A,B) pairs (e.g. A=0.37pi, B=0.61pi): the value tracks 1-2xyz exactly and is neither 1 nor 0.
notes: with A = arccos x, B = arccos y, C = arccos z summing to pi, the standard identity gives x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + 2xyz = 1, so the expression equals 1 - 2xyz

working: Each of arccos x, arccos y, arccos z lies in [0, pi], so their sum can reach 3pi only if every one of them equals pi, forcing x = y = z = cos pi = -1. Then x(y+z)+y(z+x)+z(x+y) = 2(xy+yz+zx) = 2(1+1+1) = 6.

1/x = sin^2 t and 1/y = cos^2 t, so I gives sin^2 + cos^2 = 1: correct. For II write s = sin^2 t, c = cos^2 t (s+c = 1) and 1/z = 1 - sc; then 1/(xy)+1/(yz)+1/(zx) = sc + c(1-sc) + s(1-sc) = sc + (s+c) - sc(s+c) = 1: also correct. sympy simplifies both expressions to 1, and both evaluate to 1.000... at t = 0.31, 0.73, 1.19, 2.77.

x in [0, pi] puts x/2 in [0, pi/2], so cos(x/2) >= 0 and the negative option is out. cos(x/2) = sqrt((1+cos x)/2) = sqrt((1-4/5)/2) = sqrt(1/10) = 1/sqrt(10). Numerically x = 2.49809, cos(x/2) = 0.3162278 = 1/sqrt(10).

subtopic: General Solutions and Counting Solutions of Trigonometric Equations
working: cot x = sqrt(3) means tan x = 1/sqrt(3), so x = pi/6 + n*pi; the two values in [0, 2pi) are pi/6 and 7pi/6. Evaluated: cot(pi/6) = cot(7pi/6) = 1.7320508 = sqrt(3), whereas cot(5pi/6) = -sqrt(3) (kills B), cot(pi/3) = 1/sqrt(3) and 7pi/3 is outside [0, 2pi) (kills A), cot(pi/4) = 1 (kills D).

The condition gives cos t = (1 + sqrt5) sin t. Hence cos t + 4 sin t = sin t (cot t + 4) = (5 + sqrt5) sin t = sqrt5 (sqrt5 + 1) sin t = sqrt5 cos t. Numerically at t = atan(1/(1+sqrt5)) the condition holds to 1e-41 and cos t + 4 sin t = 2.1363898 = sqrt5 cos t, while 5cos t = 4.777, 5 sin t = 1.476, sqrt5 sin t = 0.660. The t+pi branch matches too, so it is not sign-dependent.

Each cosine is at most 1 in absolute value, so a sum of four of them equal to -4 forces cos(theta_i) = -1 for every i, i.e. theta_i is an odd multiple of pi. Then theta_i/2 is an odd multiple of pi/2 and cot(theta_i/2) = 0, so the sum of the four cotangents is 0.
notes: each cosine is at least -1, so a sum of four of them equal to -4 forces every theta_i = pi. Then cot(theta_i/2) = cot(pi/2) = 0 and the sum is 0

working: Reduce each allied angle: numerator = (-sin x)(-sin x)(cot x)(-cot x) = -cos^2 x; denominator = (-sin x)(cos x)(-cosec x)(-cos x) = -cos^2 x. The ratio is therefore 1. sympy simplifies the quotient to 1 and it evaluates to 1.0 at x = 0.31, 0.73, 1.19, 2.77, 5.13.

Telescope from the tail with sin2A = 2 sinA cosA: cos(pi/2^10)sin(pi/2^10) = (1/2)sin(pi/2^9), and each further cosine absorbed contributes another factor 1/2. There are 9 cosines (k = 2..10), so the product is (1/2^9) sin(pi/2) = 1/512. Evaluated directly the product is 0.001953125 = 1/512.

subtopic: Triangle Identities — A+B+C=π, Half-Angle, and Double-Angle
working: Put tanA = 2k, tanB = 3k, tanC = 4k. In any triangle tanA+tanB+tanC = tanA tanB tanC, so 9k = 24k^3 and k^2 = 3/8. Then sec^2A+sec^2B+sec^2C = 3 + (4+9+16)k^2 = 3 + 29*(3/8) = 111/8. Checked: k = sqrt6/4 gives A+B+C = pi exactly and the sum evaluates to 13.875 = 111/8.

Use cos^3 t = (cos3t + 3cos t)/4. The triple angles give cos330 + cos30 + cos390 = 3*sqrt3/2, contributing 3sqrt3/8. The linear part vanishes because 110 and 130 are 120 -/+ 10, so cos110 + cos130 = 2cos120 cos10 = -cos10, cancelling cos10. Total 3sqrt3/8; sympy returns exactly 3*sqrt(3)/8 = 0.6495191.

subtopic: Triangle Identities — A+B+C=π, Half-Angle, and Double-Angle
working: cot(B/2)cot(C/2) = sqrt(s(s-b)/((s-a)(s-c))) * sqrt(s(s-c)/((s-a)(s-b))) = s/(s-a). With b+c = 3a, s = (a+b+c)/2 = 2a and s-a = a, so the product is 2. Confirmed on three explicit triangles satisfying b+c = 3a (1,3/2,3/2), (2,7/2,5/2), (1,17/10,13/10): all give exactly 2.

subtopic: Sine and Cosine Rules — Solving Triangles
working: Sides in AP with a smallest means 2b = a + c, so a = 2b - c. Then b^2+c^2-a^2 = b^2+c^2-(2b-c)^2 = 4bc - 3b^2 = b(4c-3b), and cos A = b(4c-3b)/(2bc) = (4c-3b)/(2c). Tested on four AP triangles (2,3,4), (3,4,5), (4,4.5,5), (5,6,7): option C matches cos A every time while A, B and D each fail.

subtopic: Heights and Distances from Angles of Elevation
working: Horizontal distances from the observer are 900/tan60 = 300sqrt3 and 900/tan30 = 900sqrt3, so the plane covers 600sqrt3 m in 10 s, i.e. 60sqrt3 m/s. Converting, 60sqrt3 * 3.6 = 216sqrt3 km/h (about 374.1 km/h).

subtopic: Heights and Distances from Angles of Elevation
working: Taking the 40 s from the first sighting: horizontal distance = 300sqrt3 + 60sqrt3*40 = 2700sqrt3, so tan(elevation) = 900/(2700sqrt3) = 1/(3sqrt3) (about 10.89 degrees). Reading the 40 s from the second sighting instead gives tan = sqrt3/11, which matches none of the four options, so the first reading is the intended one.

All three vertices lie on the circle of radius a centred at the origin, so for an equilateral triangle the centroid coincides with that centre: (a/3)(sum cos) = 0 and (a/3)(sum sin) = 0. Equivalently the angles differ by 2pi/3 and sum exp(i(t+2pi k/3)) = exp(it)(1+w+w^2) = 0. Checked numerically at start angles 0, 0.17pi, 1.19, 4.77 in both orientations: both sums are 0 to 1e-41 while the three side lengths stay equal. Both statements hold.
notes: Printed options (A) and (B) are identical -- both read "Only I"; (B) was presumably meant to be "Only II". The answer is unaffected because the correct response "Both I and II" appears once, as (C).

working: I is false: the area of an equilateral triangle of side s is (sqrt3/4)s^2, irrational for s = 1, so it is not a rational number in general. II is true (Euler line): on the triangle (0,0),(6,0),(1,4) sympy gives O=(3,11/8), G=(7/3,4/3), H=(1,5/4), collinear with OG:GH = 1:2. III is true: solving the two equidistance equations yields the single point (3,11/8), the circumcentre. So II and III only.

AB and AD meet only at the origin, so A = (0,0); since 11x+7y = 9 does not pass through A it must be the diagonal BD. Intersecting it with 4x+5y = 0 and 7x+2y = 0 gives B = (5/3,-4/3) and D = (-2/3,7/3), whose midpoint is (1/2,1/2). The other diagonal AC joins (0,0) to that midpoint, so its equation is y = x, i.e. x - y = 0. (C = B+D-A = (1,1) satisfies x-y = 0 and none of the other three options.)

With A = (0,0), B = (5/3,-4/3), D = (-2/3,7/3) the area is the cross product |x_B*y_D - x_D*y_B| = |35/9 - 8/9| = 3 sq units. Cross-checked by the shoelace formula on A, B, C = (1,1), D, which also gives 3; C lies on 7x+2y = 9 and 4x+5y = 9, confirming BC || AD and DC || AB.

subtopic: Angle Between Lines, Parallelism, and Perpendicularity
working: The line x cos(t) + y sin(t) = 2 has normal (cos t, sin t); x - y = 3 has normal (1, -1). Two lines are perpendicular iff their normals are, so cos t - sin t = 0, i.e. tan t = 1, t = pi/4 (+ n*pi). Checked all four options: only pi/4 gives normal dot product 0 (pi/6 gives 0.366, pi/2 gives -1, pi/3 gives -0.366).
Substitute into L(x,y) = 3x - 5y + 7. L(2,1) = 6 - 5 + 7 = 8 and L(3,-1) = 9 + 5 + 7 = 21. Both strictly positive, so neither point is on the line and both lie on the same side.

subtopic: Circle Equation — Centre, Radius, Diameter, and Properties
working: Equal area means equal radius. For x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0, r^2 = g^2+f^2-c. I: g=2, f=-3, c=-12 gives r^2 = 4+9+12 = 25. II: g=-6, f=-7, c=60 gives r^2 = 36+49-60 = 25. III: g=-5, f=4, c=18 gives r^2 = 25+16-18 = 23. So I and II both have r = 5 while III has r = sqrt(23); the equal-area pair is I and II.

subtopic: Parabola — Equation, Properties, and Latus Rectum
working: Complete the square: y^2 - 2y = 2x - 5 gives (y-1)^2 = 2(x-2), a rightward parabola with vertex (2,1) and 4a = 2 so a = 1/2. Focus = (2 + 1/2, 1) = (5/2, 1) and directrix x = 2 - 1/2 = 3/2. Verified the focus-directrix property at four points of the curve (y = 1, 3, -2, 5): distance to (5/2,1) equals distance to x = 3/2 exactly in each case. So (B) holds; the focus is (5/2,1) not (1,2), which kills (C), and (D)'s directrix is wrong.

subtopic: Ellipse — Foci, Eccentricity, and Focal Distances
working: Distance between foci 2ae = 8 gives ae = 4; distance between directrices 2a/e = 25 gives a/e = 25/2. Multiplying, a^2 = 4 * 25/2 = 50, so a = 5*sqrt(2) and the major axis 2a = 10*sqrt(2). Back-check with e = 4/(5*sqrt(2)) = 2*sqrt(2)/5: 2ae = 8.000000 and 2a/e = 25.000000 exactly.
notes: 2ae = 8 and 2a/e = 25 give ae = 4 and a/e = 12.5, whose product is a^2 = 50. So a = 5*sqrt2 and the major axis 2a = 10*sqrt2

working: Semi-conjugate axis b = 2*sqrt(3) so b^2 = 12. Latus rectum 2b^2/a = 12 gives 24/a = 12, a = 2. Then e^2 = 1 + b^2/a^2 = 1 + 12/4 = 4, e = 2. The rival reading (full conjugate axis = 2*sqrt(3), b^2 = 3, a = 1/2) would give e = sqrt(13), which matches no option, confirming the semi-axis reading is the intended one.

Direction cosines satisfy cos^2(a) + cos^2(b) + cos^2(g) = 1. With a = 45 and b = 120: 1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4, so cos^2(g) = 1/4 and cos(g) = +/- 1/2, i.e. g = 60 or 120 degrees. The acute value is 60 degrees.

I: a = 30, b = 45 gives cos^2 sum = 3/4 + 1/2 = 5/4 > 1, so cos^2(g) would have to be negative and no such line exists; with g = 150 the three squares total 2, not 1. I is false. subtopic: Differentiability of Absolute Value, Piecewise, and Greatest Integer Functions
working: The denominator 1 + |x| is never zero. For x > 0, f = x/(1+x) with f' = 1/(1+x)^2; for x < 0, f = x/(1-x) with f' = 1/(1-x)^2. At x = 0 the difference quotient is (h/(1+|h|))/h = 1/(1+|h|) -> 1 from both sides, so f'(0) = 1 exists; both one-sided derivatives equal 1. The modulus creates no corner because the kink sits in the denominator and is multiplied by the vanishing numerator x. So f is differentiable on all of R, with f'(x) = 1/(1+|x|)^2 (numerically confirmed at x = -2, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 3).
notes: f(x) = x/(1+|x|) has derivative 1/(1+x)^2 for x > 0 and 1/(1-x)^2 for x < 0, both tending to 1 at the origin, and f is continuous there — so it is differentiable on the whole line. Confirmed with a one-sided difference quotient at 40-digit precision: both sides give 1.000000
